1 Introduction

This project uses the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset to compare three supervised machine-learning classifiers: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine (SVM). The target variable, Outcome, has two classes: 0 (no diabetes) and 1 (diabetes).

This is an academic demonstration. The models are not medical diagnostic tools and must not be used to make healthcare decisions.

2 Aim and objectives

The aim is to investigate whether machine-learning models can classify the diabetes outcome using the available biomedical measurements.

The objectives are to:

  • inspect and explore the dataset;
  • handle zero values used as missing-value codes;
  • divide the data into training and testing subsets;
  • train Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and SVM;
  • evaluate and compare the models;
  • present the findings using tables and visualisations.

3 Dataset

The dataset contains 768 observations and nine columns: eight input variables and one target variable.

The input variables are Pregnancies, Glucose, BloodPressure, SkinThickness, Insulin, BMI, DiabetesPedigreeFunction, and Age. The target variable is Outcome.

The dataset contains 500 records with Outcome 0 and 268 records with Outcome 1. It represents Pima Indian women aged 21 years or older, so the findings should not automatically be generalised to other populations.

4 Data preprocessing and methodology

Zero values in Glucose, BloodPressure, SkinThickness, Insulin, and BMI were treated as missing-value codes. Zero pregnancies was retained because it is a valid value. Missing values were replaced using medians calculated from the training data.

The data was split into training and testing subsets using a stratified 80:20 split with random seed 123. The training set contained 615 observations and the test set contained 153 observations.

Three classification algorithms were evaluated:

  • Logistic Regression: a binary classification baseline that estimates the probability of the diabetes outcome.
  • Random Forest: an ensemble of decision trees that can model non-linear patterns.
  • Support Vector Machine: a classifier that identifies a separating decision boundary between classes.

7 Results and discussion

Random Forest achieved the highest accuracy (82.35%), recall (67.92%), F1-score (72.73%), and balanced accuracy (78.96%) in this experiment. Logistic Regression achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.8904) and specificity (91.00%). SVM achieved an accuracy of 79.08% and ROC-AUC of 0.8832.

These results show why it is important to compare several evaluation measures rather than relying only on accuracy. In particular, Random Forest still missed 17 of the 53 actual diabetes cases in the test set. Its recall was 67.92%, so the model should not be considered suitable for clinical screening without substantial further validation.

8 Limitations

The dataset is relatively small and represents a specific population: Pima Indian women aged 21 years or older. The results are based on one train/test split and may change with another split. The models also make some incorrect predictions, including false negatives. External validation, repeated cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and evaluation on more representative data would be useful future work.

The project is for learning and research purposes only. It is not a validated clinical decision-support system.

9 Conclusion

The project completed a supervised machine-learning workflow in R, including data inspection, preprocessing, exploratory analysis, model training, evaluation, and visualisation. Among the tested models, Random Forest achieved the strongest results on accuracy, recall, F1-score, and balanced accuracy, while Logistic Regression achieved the highest ROC-AUC and specificity.

The findings apply only to this dataset and test split. They should not be interpreted as medical advice or a diagnosis.

10 Reproducibility

The analysis script is available at code/diabetes_analysis.R. Generated figures are stored in figures/, while model comparison tables, confusion matrices, imputation medians, saved models, and R session information are stored in report/.
